Quality control helps determine whether materials and products meet approved quality
requirements. It includes appropriate sampling, specifications, testing, documentation and review. Quality
cannot be assured by final testing alone, so laboratory controls work
alongside manufacturing controls. Quality control activities should be independent where required
by the applicable quality system and regulations.
A specification describes tests, analytical procedures and acceptance criteria for a
material or product. Approved methods should be suitable for their intended
use, with validation or verification as appropriate. Analysts must use current
controlled procedures and suitable reference standards. Results should be compared against
the actual approved specification, not an assumed industry-wide number.
Sampling plans should consider the material, process, risk and intended test.
Samples must be appropriately identified, collected, handled and stored to preserve
integrity. A result from a poorly selected or compromised sample may
not represent the batch. Sampling procedures and any required environmental controls
should be defined and followed. Traceability links each sample to its
source and analysis.
Laboratory instruments must be suitable for their intended measurements. Qualification, calibration,
maintenance and system suitability checks may be needed depending on the
equipment and method. Analysts should verify instrument status before use and
preserve relevant records. A successful system suitability check does not automatically
excuse overdue calibration or missing qualification evidence.
An out-of-specification result, often called O O S, occurs when a
result falls outside an established acceptance criterion. Such results require timely,
documented evaluation under applicable procedures. A laboratory investigation may examine potential
analytical errors, while the wider assessment considers manufacturing and product impact
where appropriate. Retesting must follow justified approved procedures and must not
be used simply to obtain a passing result.
Laboratory data must be attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate, with
additional expectations for completeness, consistency, endurance and availability. Electronic raw data,
audit trails, calculations and relevant metadata should be controlled according to
risk and applicable requirements. Transcribing a final number without retaining required
underlying data may undermine traceability and review.
Batch disposition decisions rely on more than a passing laboratory result.
Authorized personnel should evaluate relevant manufacturing records, deviations, testing results, specifications
and other required evidence. Responsibilities and legal release requirements vary by
jurisdiction and product. A laboratory analyst should not independently declare a
batch releasable merely because a single test passed.
Imagine a finished-product assay result outside its approved specification. The analyst
should preserve the original data and promptly report the result according
to the laboratory procedure. Authorized personnel should conduct an appropriate investigation
and assess possible batch impact. The result must not be deleted,
averaged away or replaced by an unjustified repeat test. The documented
outcome informs the final quality decision.
